node.date_label: Sutherland 1976 · Parr, ed., 1982 · Rooke and Schnell 1983 · 1990s expansion (Comacchio 1993 to Gleason 1999; Marshall 1998) · selected publication milestones, not boundaries; coverage through 2000

date_span.basis: Selected publication milestones only. 1976 is the earliest selected Canadian monograph, not a field origin; 1999 is the last selected in-period work. Post-2000 work sits in extension_coverage.

node.description: Studies children, adolescents and families in Canadian history, and the reformers, experts, courts, schools and welfare programmes that sought to shape them. Neil Sutherland's Children in English-Canadian Society (1976) traced the reformers who pursued social improvement through children. Parr's study of British child immigrants (1980) and her collection Childhood and Family in Canadian History (1982), Rooke and Schnell's history of child rescue and the welfare state (1983) and Bradbury's family economies of industrial Montreal (1993) tied the field to family and labour history. The 1990s brought studies of maternal and infant welfare (Comacchio 1993), the baby boom (Owram 1996), youth and the making of heterosexuality (Adams 1997) and psychology and the 'normal' family (Gleason 1999). Francophone work examined family allowances and compulsory schooling (Marshall 1998), juvenile reform schools (Ménard 2003) and the medicalization of motherhood (Baillargeon 2004). Comacchio treats adolescence as a sociohistorical construction (2006); Myers studies girls, the courts and the policing of children in Montreal and beyond (2006, 2019). John Bullen's review essay on recent approaches to child-welfare history (1985) is the one early critique found. Historians also ask how young people's own experience can be recovered: Sutherland on adult memories of childhood (1992), and Gleason's critique of 'agency traps' (2016). The field overlaps with women's and gender history and with moral regulation; residential schooling of Indigenous children is treated primarily in the Native–newcomer entry.
node.scope_note: A research field defined by its topic (the user's 'topic field', 2026-10-12; entry_type follows the atlas vocabulary). It combines histories of children, youth and family with histories of child welfare, health, schooling and juvenile justice. Rosters overlap heavily with cdn_women_gender and moral_regulation; roster inclusion is not an exclusive placement. Indigenous childhood and residential schools are left to native_newcomer and settler_colonialism; a comparison edge to native_newcomer (ccy_rel_04, citing Milloy) cross-references them.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Sutherland, Children in English-Canadian Society (1976); Parr, Labouring Children (1980) and ed., Childhood and Family in Canadian History (1982); Rooke and Schnell, Discarding the Asylum (1983); Bullen, "Orphans, Idiots, Lunatics, and Historians" (1985), review essay; Bradbury, ed., Canadian Family History (1992) and Working Families (1993); Chunn, From Punishment to Doing Good (1992); Comacchio, "Nations Are Built of Babies" (1993) and The Infinite Bonds of Family (1999); Owram, Born at the Right Time (1996); Adams, The Trouble with Normal (1997); Sutherland, Growing Up (1997); Marshall, Aux origines sociales de l'État-providence (1998); Gleason, Normalizing the Ideal (1999). Extension: Sangster, Girl Trouble (2002); Ménard, Des enfants sous surveillance (2003); Baillargeon, Un Québec en mal d'enfants (2004); Comacchio, The Dominion of Youth (2006); Myers, Caught (2006) and Youth Squad (2019); Gleason et al., eds., Lost Kids (2010); Gleason, Small Matters (2013) and "Avoiding the Agency Trap" (2016).

strands.title: Reformers, child rescue and the welfare state
strands.focus: Reformers, child-saving institutions and the turn to state welfare; reform is the object of study, not a celebrated cause. Bullen's 1985 review essay is the one contemporary critique found (unread).
strands.works: Neil Sutherland, Children in English-Canadian Society: Framing the Twentieth-Century Consensus (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1976; reissued Waterloo: Wilfrid Laurier University Press, 2000).; Patricia T. Rooke and R. L. Schnell, Discarding the Asylum: From Child Rescue to the Welfare State in English-Canada (1800–1950) (Lanham, MD: University Press of America, 1983).; John Bullen, “Orphans, Idiots, Lunatics, and Historians: Recent Approaches to the History of Child Welfare in Canada,” Histoire sociale/Social History 18, no. 35 (May 1985): 133–45.; Dominique Marshall, Aux origines sociales de l'État-providence: familles québécoises, obligation scolaire et allocations familiales, 1940–1955 (Montréal: Presses de l'Université de Montréal, 1998).; Dominique Marshall, The Social Origins of the Welfare State: Quebec Families, Compulsory Education, and Family Allowances, 1940–1955, trans. strands.focus: Psychology, schooling and heterosexual norms; the baby boom as a generation. Overlaps moral_regulation and cdn_sixties.
strands.works: Doug Owram, Born at the Right Time: A History of the Baby-Boom Generation (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1996).; Mary Louise Adams, The Trouble with Normal: Postwar Youth and the Making of Heterosexuality (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1997).; Mona Gleason, Normalizing the Ideal: Psychology, Schooling, and the Family in Postwar Canada (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1999).

strands.title: Juvenile justice, delinquency and policing
strands.focus: Family courts, reform schools, girls before the courts and the policing of children, in English Canada and Quebec.
strands.works: Dorothy E. Chunn, From Punishment to Doing Good: Family Courts and Socialized Justice in Ontario, 1880–1940 (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1992).; Joan Sangster, Girl Trouble: Female Delinquency in English Canada (Toronto, 2002).; Sylvie Ménard, Des enfants sous surveillance: la rééducation des jeunes délinquants au Québec (1840–1950) (Montréal: VLB éditeur, 2003).; Tamara Myers, Caught: Montreal's Modern Girls and the Law, 1869–1945 (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 2006).; Tamara Gene Myers, Youth Squad: Policing Children in the Twentieth Century (Montreal and Kingston: McGill-Queen's University Press, 2019).

strands.title: Memory, agency and evidence
strands.focus: How historians recover young people's experience: adult memories of childhood, vulnerable children, and Gleason's critique of contributory, binaried and undifferentiated approaches to agency.
strands.works: Neil Sutherland, "When You Listen to the Winds of Childhood, How Much Can You Believe?" Curriculum Inquiry 22, no. 3 (1992): 235–256.; Neil Sutherland, Growing Up: Childhood in English Canada from the Great War to the Age of Television (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1997).; Mona Gleason, Tamara Myers, Leslie Paris and Veronica Strong-Boag, eds., Lost Kids: Vulnerable Children and Youth in Twentieth-Century Canada and the United States (Vancouver: UBC Press, 2010).; Mona Gleason, "Avoiding the Agency Trap: Caveats for Historians of Children, Youth, and Education," History of Education 45, no. 4 (2016): 446–459.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Childhood and family as historical subjects
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: The demography umbrella's strand on childhood evidence (Ariès; Pollock) and its household studies can be read alongside Canadian childhood and family history, which grew from social and family history (Parr, ed., 1982; Bradbury, ed., 1992) more than from family reconstitution. PhD context: 12 of 132 PhDs engaging this group cite Ariès (9% vs 3%; lift 2.96). Comparison; no descent from Ariès is asserted.

Much of the childhood and family field grew within women's history: Strong-Boag on girls and women (1988), Bradbury on family economies (1993), Comacchio on saving mothers and children (1993), Baillargeon on the medicalization of maternity (2004). Shared people are rosters, not edges. PhD context: 50 of 54 2009–2026 PhDs engaging cdn_childhood_youth also engage cdn_women_gender (93%; lift 3.94), counted after removing shared anchors (Bradbury, Comacchio, Korinek, Strong-Boag). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs.

proposed_relationships.relationship: The baby boom as a generation
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Owram's history of the baby-boom generation (1996) is the most-cited work for this group's engaged PhDs and also anchors cdn_sixties. Title-level. PhD context: 49 of 107 2009–2026 PhDs engaging cdn_childhood_youth also engage cdn_sixties (46%; lift 4.06), counted after removing shared anchors (Owram). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Indigenous children and the residential school system
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Milloy's history of the residential school system follows a government system whose underfunding affected 'the health, education, and well-being of entire generations of Aboriginal children' (publisher description). The Canadian childhood field leaves residential schooling to the Native–newcomer entry; this edge cross-references the two rather than claiming the residential-school literature for childhood history. PhD context: 34% of the 44 PhDs citing A National Crime engage childhood history (lift 3.4). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

relationships_considered_not_proposed.reason: Residential schooling is cross-referenced once, by the comparison with native_newcomer (ccy_rel_04, answers Q43); a second edge to settler_colonialism would duplicate it.
Marshall, Ménard, Baillargeon and Myers are Quebec studies, but no checked text frames them against Quebec historiography.
Comacchio, Baillargeon and Gleason on health fit; framing unchecked.
Parr (1980) and Bradbury (1993) on child labour and family economies; covered via cdn_women_gender → cdn_working_class.

open_questions: Period: period_3 (expansion) as in groups.json, or period_2 (Sutherland 1976, Parr 1982)?
Should 'family' stay in the label? Family history also sits in the atlas's demography umbrella and in cdn_women_gender (Bradbury, Parr).
Indigenous childhood and residential schools are left to native_newcomer/settler_colonialism. Should a cross-reference strand be added here?

Critics: no published critique of the Canadian field as a whole was checked. Gleason (2016) is a critique of approaches to agency from within. Rooke and Schnell's relation to Sutherland's 'consensus' is unread. Is a critic row needed?
Owram is primary in cdn_intellectual_cultural and his book also anchors cdn_sixties; keep him here as a roster row only (proposed)?

question_resolutions.summary: Period stays period_3 (the field's most-cited works date from 1993–2000, median 1998); Sutherland 1976 and Parr 1982 remain earlier roots in the date label.
'Family' stays in the label: family is a growing dissertation topic (titles rise from 1.2% to 2.7% of PhDs).

Added comparison edge ccy_rel_04 (cdn_childhood_youth – native_newcomer) citing Milloy, A National Crime (1999), with the publisher description checked and the PhD evidence (34% of citing PhDs engage childhood history, lift 3.4); the scope note and the considered-not-proposed list point to it.

Added John Bullen's 1985 review essay (HS/SH 18, no. 35: 133–45; metadata checked via PubMed and OpenAlex) as the one known contemporary critique, with a critic row that does not describe its unread content. Rooke and Schnell keep their dates and publisher, and no claim is made that they argued against Sutherland.

The data suggest cdn_sixties as Owram's primary placement (Born at the Right Time, 70 PhDs), but the change is held for the user; his roster row here is unchanged. Applied after the user decision 2026-10-12: doug_owram primary placement is now cdn_sixties; roster rows kept.
